reading.rtitle: From an Idea to Your Living Room
paras: Every Saturday night, a singing show is watched by millions of people, and almost nobody thinks about how it is made. Most of the work is invisible, and a lot of it starts in another country. The format was created in the Netherlands and was sold to dozens of countries. That means that the rules, the red chairs and even the order of the rounds are decided by the people who own the format, not by the local team. The local team decides everything else, and everything else is a lot.

Pre-production starts months before the first episode. Singers are found in auditions all over the country, and only a few of them are invited back. Songs are chosen with each singer, and then every song has to be cleared: permission is requested from the people who own it. If a song is not cleared in time, it is cut, and the singer is asked to choose another one. Rehearsals are scheduled around the band, the coaches and the studio, and the schedule changes almost every day.

On the day of a live show, a call sheet is sent to the whole crew the night before. It says who is needed, where, and at what time. During the show, every minute is controlled by the run of show, a document that is checked and changed until the last second. Hours of footage are recorded by fifteen cameras, and the music is mixed live for the audience at home.

Then post-production begins. The footage is edited, the music is mixed again, and the colors are corrected. A ninety-minute episode is made from about ten hours of material, so most of what was recorded is never seen. When the episode airs, the credits roll for about thirty seconds. Notice how often this text does not say who did the work. That is not an accident. In production, the work usually matters more than the name, and English has a structure for exactly that.

choices: To argue that singing shows are too expensive to make.
To describe the steps that turn a format into an episode, and how much of the work is never seen.
To explain how a singer can win a television competition.

items.situation: Say where your show is recorded, without saying who records it.
tips: Our show is recorded in a big studio outside the city.
is + participle: the place matters, not the people.

items.situation: Say when the call sheet is sent on your team.
tips: The call sheet is sent to the crew the night before.
Present passive for a routine that happens every week.

items.situation: Say what happened to a song that was not cleared, last season.
tips: It was cut, and the singer was asked to choose another one.
Past passive: was + participle, for one finished event.

items.situation: Ask a question about the footage, in the passive.
tips: How many hours of footage are recorded for one episode?

items.situation: Say something that was decided by the people who own the format.
tips: The order of the rounds was decided by the format owners.
Add by only when the person really matters.

items.situation: Describe one step of post-production on a project of yours.
tips: The vocals are tuned first, and then the whole song is mixed again.
Two passives in one sentence: the process, step by step.

listenings.text: Every song that you hear on a singing show has been through my desk. My job is rights clearance. When a contestant chooses a song, a request is sent to the publisher, and the song is cleared only when the permission comes back in writing. Most requests are answered in a week. Some are never answered at all. Last season, a song was chosen for the semi-final on a Monday, and the permission was refused on Thursday, two days before the show. The singer was told that night. A new song was chosen, a new arrangement was written in twenty-four hours, and the band rehearsed it on Friday morning. On Saturday it was sung live, and nobody watching at home knew that it was the second choice. People think the hard part of television is the cameras. For me, the hard part is a piece of paper that is signed by somebody I have never met.

I edit a ninety-minute episode, and I start with about ten hours of footage. That means that almost everything that is recorded is never seen. People ask me if that is sad. It is not. It is the job. On a live show, the footage is recorded by fifteen cameras, and every camera is logged by an assistant while the show is happening. By Sunday morning the best moments are marked, and the first version is cut by Sunday night. Then it is watched by the producers, and they always ask for the same thing: shorter. Whole performances are cut because they arrive at the wrong moment in the story. The hardest one I ever cut was a duet which was perfect. It was simply too long, and it was removed in the last version. The singers never asked me about it. I think they never knew how well it was filmed.

extra_audio.text: The format was bought from the company that created it. Singers were found in auditions all over the country. Every song was cleared before the first rehearsal. The call sheet was sent to the crew the night before. Hours of footage were recorded by fifteen cameras. The episode was edited, and it aired on Saturday night.
